damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (Great Hall feast speech) - Dumbledore's opening remarks
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 12-17: Dumbledore opens with 'Welcome to another year at Hogwarts! I have a few things to say, and as one of them is very serious, I think it best to get it out of the way before you become befuddled by our excellent feast.' He leads with gravity, addresses the dementors first with clear solemnity, pausing to look 'very seriously around the hall' so that 'nobody moved or made a sound.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 1: Dumbledore opens with a jovial joke about 'flaming kiwi cups' being 'somewhat treacherous for those of us with facial hair,' requiring McGonagall to clear her throat to redirect him. The serious dementor announcement comes last rather than first, framed as an afterthought after the staff introductions.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book establishes that Dumbledore deliberately prioritises the serious warning before the feast, demonstrating his protective instincts and authoritative judgment. The film reorders this to make him appear bumbling and in need of correction by McGonagall, undermining his commanding gravitas and the trust Harry immediately feels in him. The book's Harry feels 'really calm for the first time since the dementor had entered the train compartment' specifically because of how Dumbledore carries himself; that effect is weakened when he opens with a joke that requires a colleague to steer him back on track.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (Great Hall feast speech) - Dementor warning tone and content
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 13-16: Dumbledore warns the students with explicit authority and controlled disapproval: 'I must make it plain that nobody is to leave school without permission... I therefore warn each and every one of you to give them no reason to harm you.' Book Scene 14 notes Harry remembers Dumbledore 'not being happy' about the dementors, conveying his restrained but clear resistance to their presence. Book Scene 79: Dumbledore states coldly, 'no dementor will cross the threshold of this castle while I am headmaster.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 1: The film omits Dumbledore's personal displeasure with the dementors entirely from the speech. He presents their presence as a straightforward Ministry arrangement ('at the request of the Ministry of Magic') without any of the book's undercurrent of reluctance or protective defiance. The cold declaration that no dementor will enter the castle while he is headmaster is absent from the feast scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book establishes Dumbledore as a figure who complies with Ministry requirements while making his own protective limits crystal clear. His personal displeasure with the dementors is a character beat that shows his moral compass operating independently of political pressure. The film's version makes him appear a neutral administrator passing on Ministry instructions, losing the dimension of principled resistance that defines him throughout this book.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (Fat Lady portrait / Great Hall sleepover) - Dumbledore's command of the crisis
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 40-55: Dumbledore arrives sweeping through the crowd, immediately issues precise orders to McGonagall and Filch, calmly interrogates Peeves (who 'didn't dare taunt Dumbledore'), and with one casual wave of his wand rearranges the entire Great Hall into a dormitory. He manages the castle search through the night, speaks with Snape at 3 a.m. with quiet authority, and shuts down Snape's insinuation about Lupin with a tone that makes 'it so clear that the subject was closed that Snape didn't reply.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 3-5: Dumbledore's instructions are compressed. He tells Filch to 'round up the ghosts' (a change from the book's McGonagall/Filch division of labour), and the overnight search scene is condensed. The film does retain his dismissal of Snape's insinuation about Lupin, but the extended demonstration of Dumbledore as the calm, methodical, magically powerful centre of the crisis response is significantly compressed, including the wand-wave that furnishes the hall.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses the Fat Lady crisis as a showcase for exactly why everyone trusts Dumbledore: he is unhurried, authoritative, magically capable, and politically clear-sighted under pressure. The film's compression reduces him to a few lines of instruction, losing the cumulative effect of watching him manage a genuine security emergency with total competence. The missing wand-wave furnishing the hall is a small but characteristic expression of his effortless power.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 (Quidditch match / Harry falls) - Dumbledore's intervention
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 84-85: Hermione recounts that 'Dumbledore was really angry... I've never seen him like that before. He ran onto the field as you fell, waved his wand, and you sort of slowed down before you hit the ground. Then he whirled his wand at the dementors. Shot silver stuff at them. They left the stadium right away... He was furious they'd come onto the grounds.' The anger is described as unprecedented and directed at a genuine breach of his authority.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 6: The film shows Dumbledore as 'a tall figure' who 'raises an open hand to the heavens' and produces an explosion that slows Harry's fall and repels the dementors. While the action is present, his fury is not conveyed in the scene itself — the film cuts to the hospital wing where Hermione simply says 'Dumbledore was furious. After he saved you, he sent them straight off.' The unprecedented nature of his anger, and the physical description of him running onto the field, is reduced to a reported line.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book specifically flags that students have never seen Dumbledore that angry, which is itself characterisation — it shows that beneath his serene exterior there is a fierce protectiveness that can erupt when students are endangered. The film's version renders him as a competent magical intervention rather than a furious guardian. The distinction is small but contributes to a flatter emotional portrait.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 13 (Hospital wing / Time-Turner scene) - Dumbledore's aphoristic detachment
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 209-217: Dumbledore enters the hospital wing, quickly asserts private authority by clearing the room, then speaks with precise, low urgency: 'It is your turn to listen, and I beg you will not interrupt me, because there is very little time.' He explains the legal and evidentiary problem with clinical clarity, explicitly tells Harry 'I do believe you' while explaining why he cannot act, and then gives the Time-Turner instruction with deliberate specificity ('Thirteenth window from the right of the West Tower'). His tone is grave and focused; he is solving a problem under pressure.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 13: Dumbledore enters, delivers a lyrical speech ('A child's voice, however honest and true, is meaningless to those who have forgotten how to listen'), gazes at a shooting star, and frames the Time-Turner hint as a series of poetic riddles about time being 'mysterious' and 'dangerous.' He hands out chocolate, offers the cryptic 'when in doubt, I find retracing my steps to be a wise place to begin,' and exits. The specific window location is replaced with 'topmost cell of the Dark Tower.'
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the most damaging single scene in the corpus for Dumbledore's characterisation. The book's Dumbledore is urgently practical: he trusts Harry and Hermione with precise operational information because he respects their intelligence and the stakes are high. The film replaces this with an oracular, detached persona dispensing riddles and aphorisms while staring at stars. This shift — from a trusted adult giving children the tools and information they need, to a mystical figure speaking in fortune-cookie language — misrepresents his relationship with Harry. Book Dumbledore's trust is expressed through clarity and respect; film Dumbledore's is expressed through whimsy and deliberate obscurity. It also alters the relational dynamic: Harry in the book feels the weight of Dumbledore's direct guidance; in the film he is left to decode metaphors.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 16 (Buckbeak rescue, exterior) - Dumbledore's complicit amusement
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 239: When Buckbeak vanishes, Dumbledore says 'How extraordinary' with 'a note of amusement in his voice,' then redirects the executioner's attention: 'Search the skies, if you will... Hagrid, I could do with a cup of tea. Or a large brandy.' He is clearly aware something has happened and smoothly protects the situation.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 16: Dumbledore says 'How extraordinary!' with visible amusement, protects Hagrid by noting he was present the whole time, tells the Minister to 'search the skies,' and suggests a cup of tea or brandy. He also adds a line about 'Professor Dippet had those blackberries planted' to distract Fudge's attention from Buckbeak while Harry and Hermione lead him away.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is largely faithful and the film actually adds the 'blackberries' distraction line which fits the character well. The damage here is minimal — the portrayal is consistent with the book. Scored low accordingly; included only because the corpus contains it as an explicit film beat to evaluate.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 18 (Clocktower corridor / return from time travel) - Dumbledore's reaction to success
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 262-265: Dumbledore looks up as Harry and Hermione run toward him, and 'a wide smile appeared under the long silver mustache.' When Harry reports 'Sirius has gone, on Buckbeak,' Dumbledore 'beamed at them,' said 'Well done,' then listened carefully before confirming they had succeeded. His response is warm but swift and practical.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 18: Dumbledore stops at the door, looks up, and asks 'Well?' When Harry says 'He's free — Sirius. We… we did it,' Dumbledore asks 'Did what?' with a twinkle in his eye before swinging the door open. The 'Did what?' plays as a light joke or feigned innocence.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The 'Did what?' line, while charming, tips the characterisation slightly toward the arch-trickster persona rather than the book's quietly beaming pride. It is a minor drift but consistent with the film's broader pattern of making Dumbledore more enigmatically playful and less warmly direct. Low damage on its own but part of a cumulative tonal shift.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 19 (Lupin's departure) - Dumbledore's relationship with Lupin and the Firebolt reveal
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 287-314: After Lupin's departure Dumbledore stays behind with Harry and has an extended, deeply personal conversation. He tells Harry he should be proud, explains why saving Pettigrew mattered ('It does not... You did a very noble thing'), reveals the magical bond created by saving a life, speaks gently about James Potter ('I knew your father very well'), and reflects on the Patronus: 'You know, Harry, in a way, you did see your father last night.... You found him inside yourself.' This scene establishes Dumbledore as Harry's most important adult confidant. Additionally, Book Scene 318-319 implies Dumbledore may have intervened with Snape's grading.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 19: Lupin departs after a brief exchange with Harry. There is no subsequent private scene between Dumbledore and Harry. The Firebolt arrives, apparently from Sirius (implied by the feather), skipping the book's ambiguity about Dumbledore possibly sending it (Book Scenes 119-121). The entire post-time-travel conversation in which Dumbledore gives Harry moral and emotional orientation is absent from the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the second most structurally damaging absence in the corpus. The end-of-year conversation is where Dumbledore most fully inhabits his role as Harry's mentor, moral guide, and emotional anchor — roles that define their relationship across the entire saga. He explicitly validates Harry's actions, reframes the apparent failure as genuine heroism, introduces the concept of the life-debt (which pays off in Book 4), and connects Harry to his father in a way that gives the Patronus scene its full meaning. Without this scene, Dumbledore's mentorship function in this film is largely implied rather than demonstrated, and the Harry-Dumbledore relationship loses a defining moment of intimacy and guidance.

main_damage_causes: Tonal flattening from wise-and-grave to whimsical-and-oracular: the film consistently replaces Dumbledore's urgent, practical, trust-based guidance with detached aphorisms and riddles, most damagingly in the hospital wing Time-Turner scene where precise operational direction becomes poetic misdirection.

Loss of the post-time-travel mentor conversation: the book's most explicit scene of Dumbledore as emotional anchor, moral teacher, and intimate confidant to Harry is entirely absent from the film corpus, weakening the Harry-Dumbledore relationship arc at the moment it should be most clearly established.

Erosion of commanding gravitas in crisis moments: across the feast speech, the Fat Lady incident, and the Quidditch match intervention, the film consistently compresses or softens Dumbledore's demonstrations of protective authority, displeasure, and magical power, replacing cumulative awe with a more genial and reactive figure.
